specStatements.text: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.
Electromagnetic waves form a continuous spectrum and all types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

The waves that form the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of their wavelength and their frequency. Going from long to short wavelength (or from low to high frequency) the groups are: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Our eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.
Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves.

concepts.definition: A transverse wave that transfers energy from the source of the wave to an absorber. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, so no substance is needed to carry them.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction in which the wave transfers energy. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
A wave moves energy from one place to another without moving matter from one place to another. The particles or fields oscillate; they are not carried along.
The source is the object that emits the wave; the absorber is the object that takes in its energy. A lamp is a source of light; a black surface it shines on is an absorber.

The electromagnetic spectrum has no gaps: wavelength changes smoothly from very long to very short, and the seven named groups are labelled regions of one continuous range, not seven separate wave types.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave. Radio waves have the longest wavelength in the spectrum and gamma rays the shortest.
The number of waves passing a point each second. Across the spectrum frequency rises as wavelength falls, so gamma rays have the highest frequency and radio waves the lowest.
The only group of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect. Within it, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest, so the group runs red to violet.
A space containing no matter. All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air, which is why sunlight reaches the Earth across empty space.

misconceptions.question: Do electromagnetic waves need air, or some other substance, to travel through?
misconceptions.correct: No. They travel through a vacuum (space) as well as through air.
misconceptions.misconception: A wave must have something to travel through, so light must be carried by air — there must be very thin air out in space carrying sunlight to us.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound, water waves and waves on a rope are all met before light, and every one of them needs a substance. The rule 'a wave needs a medium' is then over-generalised.
misconceptions.correction: Electromagnetic waves are the exception: they need no medium. Sunlight, infrared and ultraviolet cross millions of kilometres of empty space to reach the Earth, which they could not do if a substance were required.

misconceptions.question: Are electromagnetic waves transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: Transverse — the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
misconceptions.misconception: They are longitudinal, like sound, because they spread outwards from a source.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound is usually the first wave studied in detail, and 'spreads out from a source' is remembered as the defining feature rather than the direction of the oscillation.
misconceptions.correction: Spreading out from a source says nothing about the type of wave. All electromagnetic waves are transverse; sound is the longitudinal one.

misconceptions.question: When a wave travels from a source to an absorber, what actually arrives?
misconceptions.correct: Energy arrives. Matter is not transferred from the source to the absorber.
misconceptions.misconception: Tiny particles must travel from the source to the absorber, otherwise nothing would have been delivered.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday transfers involve something moving — post, water through a pipe — so the student looks for a substance making the journey.
misconceptions.correction: The wave transfers energy only. A radio aerial gains energy from a transmitter but gains no material from it.

misconceptions.question: Do gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum?
misconceptions.correct: No. All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum or air.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma rays are the most energetic and most dangerous, so they must be the fastest; radio waves must be the slowest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy, frequency and speed are collapsed into one idea of 'how powerful the wave is'. Danger is also read as speed.
misconceptions.correction: Speed in a vacuum is the same for every group. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency, and it is the high frequency, not high speed, that makes gamma rays hazardous.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say the electromagnetic spectrum is continuous?
misconceptions.correct: Wavelength changes smoothly across the whole spectrum, with no gaps between one group and the next.
misconceptions.misconception: There are seven separate kinds of wave with empty gaps in between, like seven rungs on a ladder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The spectrum is nearly always drawn as seven labelled boxes, and the boxes are taken to be seven distinct wave types.
misconceptions.correction: The boxes are labels for regions of one continuous range. The boundaries are conventions: there is a wavelength at which infrared merges into microwave with nothing missing in between.

misconceptions.question: Across the spectrum, do wavelength and frequency change in the same direction?
misconceptions.correct: No. As wavelength decreases, frequency increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Wavelength and frequency aren't really linked, so they change independently — across the spectrum they might both rise, both fall, or one rise while the other falls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are described as measures of the wave, and 'bigger wave' is treated as bigger in every respect at once.
misconceptions.correction: They are inversely related. Going from radio to gamma the wavelength gets shorter while the frequency gets higher — which is why the specification gives the same order twice, long to short wavelength or low to high frequency.

misconceptions.question: Where do infrared and ultraviolet sit relative to visible light?
misconceptions.correct: Infrared lies just beyond the red end (longer wavelength); ultraviolet lies just beyond the violet end (shorter wavelength).
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet comes before visible light and infrared after it, because 'ultra' sounds like it belongs with the low-energy end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefixes are not connected to the colours they name: 'infra-red' means below red and 'ultra-violet' means beyond violet, but neither is obvious from the word alone.
misconceptions.correction: Use the colour in the name. Infrared sits next to red, at longer wavelength; ultraviolet sits next to violet, at shorter wavelength.

misconceptions.question: Within visible light, which colour has the longest wavelength?
misconceptions.correct: Red. The visible group runs from red at the long-wavelength end to violet at the short-wavelength end.
misconceptions.misconception: Violet has the longest wavelength because it is the strongest, deepest-looking colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The order of the colours is memorised as a rainbow list without attaching it to wavelength, and appearance is used instead.
misconceptions.correction: The specification writes the group as 'visible light (red to violet)', which is the long-to-short wavelength order. Violet is nearest to ultraviolet, the shorter-wavelength side.

misconceptions.question: Can the human eye detect infrared or ultraviolet?
misconceptions.correct: No. Eyes only detect visible light, so they detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.
misconceptions.misconception: We can see infrared as a warm glow, and thermal camera pictures show that people see it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A glowing hot object really is visible, but that is the visible light it emits; thermal images are also shown in false colour, which suggests the eye is seeing the infrared itself.
misconceptions.correction: The camera detects infrared and converts it into a visible image for us. Without the camera there is nothing to see, because the eye responds only to the visible part of the spectrum.

misconceptions.question: Is every transfer of energy that warms something a transfer by electromagnetic waves?
misconceptions.correct: No. Conduction and convection move energy using particles of matter, not waves.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that warms up must have been warmed by radiation, so a spoon in hot tea is an example of energy transfer by an electromagnetic wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is filed under one heading, so the three transfer processes are not separated when an example is judged.
misconceptions.correction: Ask whether a wave crossed a gap. Sunlight warming a road crosses empty space, so it is electromagnetic; a spoon warms by touching the tea, which is conduction.

misconceptions.question: Are radio waves the same thing as sound waves?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radio waves are electromagnetic and travel through a vacuum; sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium.
misconceptions.misconception: A radio produces sound, so radio waves must be sound waves travelling through the air to the set.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name of the device and the output the student hears are the same word, and the invisible stage in between is not observed.
misconceptions.correction: The transmitter sends electromagnetic radio waves to the aerial. The loudspeaker then uses that energy to make sound waves in the air, which is a separate step.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes an electromagnetic wave?

options.text: A transverse wave that transfers energy from source to absorber
options.rationale: The specification defines electromagnetic waves as transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.

options.text: A longitudinal wave that transfers energy to an absorber
options.rationale: Sound is met first, so the oscillation is assumed to be along the direction of travel for every wave.

options.text: A transverse wave that transfers matter to an absorber
options.rationale: The student thinks something physical must arrive for a transfer to have happened; waves transfer energy, not matter.

options.text: A transverse wave that needs air to carry its energy
options.rationale: Over-generalised from sound and water waves, which do need a medium; electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum.

mcqs.stem: A transmitter sends radio waves to a distant aerial. What is transferred, and in which direction?

options.text: Particles of matter, from the transmitter to the aerial
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who pictures tiny pieces of the transmitter flying out to the aerial.

options.text: Energy, from the source of the wave to the absorber
options.rationale: The wave transfers energy from the source (the transmitter) to the absorber (the aerial).

options.text: Energy, carried along by the air between them
options.rationale: The student believes the air is doing the carrying, so the radio link would fail in a vacuum. It does not.

options.text: Sound, from the transmitter to the radio aerial
options.rationale: Radio waves are confused with the sound they eventually produce in a loudspeaker.

mcqs.stem: How do the speeds of radio waves, visible light and gamma rays compare in a vacuum?

options.text: Gamma rays are fastest because they carry the most energy
options.rationale: Energy is confused with speed; gamma rays carry more energy per wave but travel no faster.

options.text: Radio waves are slowest because their wavelength is longest
options.rationale: A long wavelength is read as 'covers more ground each second', which is not how the speed is fixed.

options.text: All of them travel at the same velocity in a vacuum
options.rationale: All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

options.text: Visible light is faster than the radio waves are
options.rationale: Light is the wave the student knows is fast, so it is assumed to be the fastest of them all.

mcqs.stem: The electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous. What does this mean?

options.text: It is made of seven separate waves with gaps between them
options.rationale: The seven named groups are read as seven distinct wave types rather than labelled regions of one spectrum.

options.text: It jumps in seven fixed steps like rungs on a ladder
options.rationale: A student holding m05 pictures the spectrum as discrete separate rungs, so imagines it steps in fixed jumps rather than being a continuous unbroken range.

options.text: Every group in it can be detected by the human eye
options.rationale: 'Continuous' is confused with 'complete to us'; the eye detects only the visible part.

options.text: There are no gaps between one group and the next
options.rationale: Wavelength changes smoothly across the spectrum, so the groups merge into one another with no gaps.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the electromagnetic groups in order from longest wavelength to shortest?

options.text: Radio, microwave, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, X-rays, gamma
options.rationale: Infrared and ultraviolet are swapped; 'ultra' is read as 'beyond red' rather than beyond violet.

options.text: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
options.rationale: This is the order given in the specification, going from long to short wavelength.

options.text: Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
options.rationale: The correct sequence written backwards: this is the order of increasing wavelength, not decreasing.

options.text: Radio, microwave, infrared, violet, red, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma
options.rationale: Violet is placed before red, reversing the visible range, which runs red to violet.

mcqs.stem: Moving across the spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, what happens to wavelength and frequency?

options.text: Wavelength decreases and frequency increases
options.rationale: Going from long to short wavelength is the same as going from low to high frequency.

options.text: Wavelength and frequency both increase together
options.rationale: Wavelength and frequency are treated as two names for the same 'size' of the wave.

options.text: Wavelength rises while the frequency falls
options.rationale: The direction of travel across the spectrum has been reversed; this describes gamma rays towards radio.

options.text: Both wavelength and frequency decrease
options.rationale: Both quantities are assumed to shrink together as the waves become more energetic.

mcqs.stem: A hot radiator emits infrared radiation. Why can a person in the room not see it?

options.text: The radiator is not hot enough to glow visibly yet
options.rationale: A student holding m09 thinks infrared appears as a visible warm glow, so reasons the radiator simply is not yet hot enough to glow.

options.text: The eye can see infrared, but only in a dark room
options.rationale: Night-vision images are taken as proof that people see infrared directly.

options.text: Infrared travels too fast for the eye to detect
options.rationale: Speed is offered as the reason; all electromagnetic waves travel at the same velocity in air.

options.text: Our eyes only detect visible light, not infrared
options.rationale: Eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the best example of energy being transferred by an electromagnetic wave?

options.text: A loudspeaker making the nearby air vibrate
options.rationale: Sound is a wave, but it is not electromagnetic; it needs the air to travel.

options.text: Warm air rising above a heater in a room
options.rationale: This is convection: energy is carried by moving particles, not by a wave.

options.text: Sunlight warming a dark road surface
options.rationale: The Sun is the source and the road is the absorber; energy crosses empty space as an electromagnetic wave.

options.text: A spoon warming inside a mug of hot tea
options.rationale: This is conduction through touching particles, not transfer by a wave.
